| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.

Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  
    
    Butterfly Crisis: Most U.S. Species in Decline, Skyler from Vermont
    Butterflies: Humanity's friends in need, James from Brattleboro Union High
    The missing butterflies, Mac Comet, Hanover Horton High School
    Are Butterfly Populations Diving or Thriving? Mrs. Rooker, Oklahoma City, OK
    Butterflies on the Verge of Extinction: Significant population drop over the last 20 years, Julia Calderaro, Academy of Saint Elizabeth
    Butterfly Populations Crash, With Only a Few Fluttering Upward, Brooke A, Boston
    Vanishing Wings: Most Butterflies Are Disappearing Fast, Emilia AOSE from The Academy of Saint Elizabeth
    
    
    Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article, a summary of the article, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graphs and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graph and where you can find them in the graph.
    
    The next graph will be released by Friday, September 12.  The topic will be the summer blockbuster movies.
    
    Signing off – Jamie Perrett from Salem, Utah, who loves nature’s beauty, especially butterflies, and Rachael Gorsuch from Ashville, Ohio, who is off to look for butterflies outside her school.

- **Beeswarm / dot plot** (a one-dimensional scatter of dots along a horizontal quantitative axis).

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **beeswarm-style jitter/packing** to avoid overlap of dots.
- No faceting, no stacking, and no small multiples.
- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |
| Statistical significance of species trend | Categorical/nominal (binary, as shown) | Outline/stroke around dots (“Outlined species’ trends were statistically significant”) |
| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:
- The y-position does **not** appear to encode a data variable; it is used for collision avoidance / packing only.
- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.
raw_comment:
From this graph, I noticed that there was a relatively large group of outliers of butterfly species that had a
    change in abundance of over 100%. Unlike the majority of the statistically significant species that have a
    change in abundance of -50% to -100%, 9 statistically significant species have a large increase of over 100% on
    the complete opposite side of the data plot.
    I wonder if some environmental factors or changes in specific areas could have contributed to the
    significant difference in each species' change of abundance over time, resulting in some species having a
    drastic increase in abundance while others had a drastic decrease in abundance.
    This could impact communities because if there's a significant decrease in the abundance of butterflies,
    certain species may suffer from it, for example, flowers or other insects that are predators of butterflies. A catchy headline could be "Have the last 20 years finally caught up to butterflies?"

## 1) Chart type
- **Beeswarm / dot plot** (a one-dimensional scatter of dots along a horizontal quantitative axis).

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **beeswarm-style jitter/packing** to avoid overlap of dots.
- No faceting, no stacking, and no small multiples.
- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |
| Statistical significance of species trend | Categorical/nominal (binary, as shown) | Outline/stroke around dots (“Outlined species’ trends were statistically significant”) |
| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:
- The y-position does **not** appear to encode a data variable; it is used for collision avoidance / packing only.
- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.

raw_comment:
The main thing I notice about the graph is that most butterfly populations are going down. I also see that the colors go from red dots on the left (more endangered species) to green dots on the right (populations increasing).
    
    One question I have is: what is causing these butterfly populations to decrease? Do these butterflies share anything in common that might explain why their numbers are dropping?
    
    This matters to my environment because butterflies are an important part of our ecosystem. My high school has a garden with many monarch butterflies that help take care of milkweed and other plants. If the butterflies disappear, these plants, especially milkweed, might not survive. We use vegetables and fruits from the garden in our lunches and science classes. The graph shows we need to watch out for our butterflies.
    
    A good name for the graph would be "Fallen Flies."

raw_comment:
What Do You Notice?
     I notice that the graph is about changes in different Butterfly populations from 2000-2020. One observation is that each dot in the graph represents a different Butterfly species. Another observation is colored dots on the left are red while the colored dots on the right are green. The green shows an increase in population and the red shows a decrease in population. The graph also has percentages on the top. in the graph on both sides it shows 100%. For the dots on the left the 100% means a 100% decrease in population and therefore extinction. the 100% for the dots on the right means a 100% increase in population. There is also a lot of dots in the middle with no color which means that those specific species have not experienced any significant change in population. 
    
    What Do You Wonder?
    There are many questions that could be asked about this graph. I wonder why there are so many Butterfly species have lost their population. I wonder if this is due to human mistakes. I also wonder if there is something that we can do to help. 
    
    How Does It Relate To You And Your Community?
    This graph relates to my community because besides Bees, Butterflies are also natural pollinators. Without them, my community can suffer from less pollination and plant and flower growth. As well as that, Butterflies are a food source. Without them, animals like birds in my community could starve as a result.
    
    Catchy Headline
    Fluttering Away: Just What is Happening to Butterflies?

## 1) Chart type
- **Beeswarm / dot plot** (a one-dimensional scatter of dots along a horizontal quantitative axis).

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **beeswarm-style jitter/packing** to avoid overlap of dots.
- No faceting, no stacking, and no small multiples.
- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |
| Statistical significance of species trend | Categorical/nominal (binary, as shown) | Outline/stroke around dots (“Outlined species’ trends were statistically significant”) |
| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:
- The y-position does **not** appear to encode a data variable; it is used for collision avoidance / packing only.
- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.

raw_comment:
I noticed that this graph represents the change in population of every single butterfly species. There are many more species of butterflies losing population and going extinct rather than gaining population. The closer you are to the -100% mark, the closer you are to extinction. On the other side of the graph, the closer you are to the 100% mark, the closer you are to doubling your species population since 2000. The species on the right grew in population, unlike the species on the left. This graph is trying to show us the dire decline in population for most butterfly species.
    
    Lots of things in this graph make me wonder. What is the difference between the species that double in population in comparison to the ones that are about to become extinct? I wonder how there are so many more species in the red zone than in the green zone. What led to the population decrease? Was it natural causes, or prey hunting? Bad Natural habitats or even us humans? 
    
    This graph can relate to us as a community. Some deaths of these species could be natural, but not all of them. We as humans aren't doing our job as people on this earth to take care of this planet, and we could have prevented some of these deaths if we just did our job. People love butterflies because of their pretty looks, and others because of their unique colors. None of these people would kill a butterfly on purpose, but that doesn’t mean that things could happen, and air pollution is a primary example.
    
    Are we the problem?

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? 
    When I examine the graph, I notice that most butterfly species have hugely declined between 2000 and 2020. The majority of dots fall on the negative side of the graph, especially in the –25% to –75% range, and they are mostly orange or reddish, showing loss. A few green points appear on the positive side, representing the species that grew, but these are much less common. Overall, the visual makes it clear that more butterfly species are shrinking in number than expanding.
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    This raises many questions for me. What exactly is driving such a sharp decline? Is it pollution, climate change, habitat destruction, or a mix of all of those things? Why do only some species seem to thrive while the majority struggle? Is it possible that humans are the reason for this sudden decline in butterfly populations? Or is it simply natural selection, and some species are better adapted to changing environments than others? 
    
    3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
    Butterflies help keep ecosystems balanced. They are also a food source for countless critters and other insects. A decline in their numbers could mean our ecosystem can face countless repercussions (and we won't have so many beautiful flowers or butterflies in our gardens anymore). 
    
    4. Catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    From Flying to Dying: Why Are So Many Butterflies On The Decline?

This is shown by the color of the dots turning into a gradually darker shade of red the further they are on the left (negative) side of the graph. I also notice the number of species that have grown in population is very little in comparison to the species that have shown a population decline.

|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |
| Statistical significance of species trend | Categorical/nominal (binary, as shown) | Outline/stroke around dots (“Outlined species’ trends were statistically significant”) |
| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

- **Beeswarm / dot plot** (a one-dimensional scatter of dots along a horizontal quantitative axis).

- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

|---|---|---|

| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:

- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.
raw_comment:
In this graph i notice a variety of colors and dots. Each dot representing a species, and the percentages representing the population. The orange dots at the very left seem like they are closer to becoming extinct, while the green ones on the right are the most abundant.
    
    I wonder why so many species are so close to extinction, compared to the species that are abundant. Im wondering if its due to something like global warming, or humans being invasive to their habitats
    
    I can relate to this because butterflies are pollinators, and as well as a food source for other animals, so the death of butterflies can have impact on the community.   
    
    Headline: The slow disappearance of Butterflies

raw_comment:
Question 1: What I noticed first is the numbers that's shown within the chart. It goes from the abundance being shown to be far less to being far more. This only shows me that the butterfly abundance is near extinct; which is shown by the orange dot that's outlined in black. While on the opposite side, the abundance is plentiful; which is shown by the green dots. However, in the middle of the scatter plot, it’s shown as grey dots –  which I believe is to symbolize that the butterfly species had no change. Since, I believe that the dots represent different butterfly populations, the graph is showing us the drastic changes that’s within the butterfly population.
    
    Question 2: What I wonder about this graph is how did the butterfly population change so drastically? Was there a disease in their food source that caused their decline? Or, was it due to human interference because of climate change?
    
    Question 3: I can relate to this graph with myself and my community. Maybe due to the fact that when the butterfly population was lower, it would’ve affected the environment because they are one of nature’s pollinators. Another way this would’ve affected the community as well, because butterflies are also a food source for other animals.
    
    Catchy Headline: Butterflies: It Takes Time to Grow your Wings

    “Butterfly Populations Crash, With Only a Few Fluttering Upward”

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph depicts the trends of butterfly abundance over the time period of 2000-2020. There is a large group of butterfly species on the left-hand side, depicted by red dots in the negatives. This means a massive majority of butterfly species have and continue to be in a population decline. The dots transition to a white color with a smaller quantity. This depicts the populations that are neutral and staying at a relatively stable number. Finally, the dots taper off and become their least abundant and a green color. This represents the number of butterfly species on the rise, and the abundance is increasing. Nearing the end, however, there is an increase in abundance past the postive 100% range.
    
    I wonder why there are so many butterfly populations that are rapidly decreasing. Is it due to environmental factors like global warming, loss of habitat, or loss of resources? Is it because of an a priori factor like a mutation or an increase in predator presence? Are the select few species that are in a rapid increase infringing on the survival rates of weaker species?
    
    This relates to me and my community because it is highly indicative of a harmful factor in the environment. Whether an invasive species or failure to survive due to loss of habitat, the loss and potential extinction of so many species in the environment is a massive concern for everyone. The loss of one species can alter and disrupt an entire food chain. 
    
    Possible title: "The Butterfly Effect"

- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

|---|---|---|

raw_comment:
In this graph I notice there are many orange dots. These dots show that species decreased over time. The dots near the -100% are most likely extinct. The closer to this percent the lesser the amount of butterflies in each specific species. As well as orange dots there are also a few green dots. These green dots show the species that populations grew. As they approached 100%, these species grew the most. Each dot represents a new species so I think this graph is trying to show us the drastic butterfly species decline.
    
    There are many things in this graph that confuse me. I wonder what the specific species are and which ones declined. I also wonder how long it took for each species to decline. Was this process fast or throughout the whole 20 years?
    
    I can relate this information from the graph to my community. Maybe there were certain factors, like pollution,  that contributed to the decrease in butterfly species. Maybe these declines could have been prevented if everyone took care of the planet. This is a good wake up call because everything has a consequence and pollution may have caused  the extinction of many beautiful butterfly species.
    
    Catchy Headline: Butterfly decline? Is it on us?

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
    This graph demonstrates the intense decline in butterfly species from the year 2000 to 2020. In this graph, most of the red colored dots indicate that the species of butterflies are decreasing. There are many more species on the side with negatives (prominently from -25 to -75.) As time goes on, only a few species continued to increase in size. 
    
    What do you wonder? 
    I wonder what the compelling factors of this decrease in butterfly species were. Was there a dramatic change in habitat or climate? Did this change in the environment emerge from humans actions? 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community? 
    This relates to my community and I because it makes me think about things I can do to help improve the environment. Instead of getting rid of natural ecosystems, is there a way to improve or create new ones that are safe? 
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    How Much Do You Care About the Environment? Butterfly Populations Are Just the Beginning

What do you notice?
    
    I noticed the steep decrease in the population of butterflies over the course of the past 20 years. What was surprising was the fact that this impact also significantly impacted such a wide variety of species. 
    
    What do you wonder?
    
    What is the underlying trend that leads to such a severe decline in the butterfly population? What impact did humans have on this situation, and are there any species that managed to thrive and grow through the adversity?

It is also interesting to consider that when I was wandering through my neighborhoods only 10 years ago, there was a much larger population of butterflies, while children now probably seldom see them. 
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    
    Butterflies on the Verge of Extinction: Significant population drop over the last 20 years

raw_comment:
It seems as though most butterfly species have experienced a population decline within the years 2000 through 2020. The left hand side of the graph (shows negative change), where it is mainly crowded with orange and red dots. In contrast, the right hand side of this graph depicts a positive change, displaying fewer green dots as it progresses. Additionally, it appears that a few species were able to increase more than 100%, but that is very scarce. As a means to prove these claims, the graph displays clusters of dots below the 0% change, which shows that the decline is more common than an increase. The outlined dots represent the different species whose declines were statistically significant. 
    
    - I wonder why there are so many different butterfly populations declining
    - Further, is this a result of climate change?
    - Additionally, what allows the few species on the right to thrive, whilst the majority of species on the left to decline? 
    
    Butterflies impact communities around the globe. This is primarily because they are pollinators, which is a significant asset to building diverse ecosystems. Therefore, if the number in their population decreases, it could negatively affect local biodiversity (plants, gardens, agriculture, etc…) Within my own community, this could result in less flowers, a disruption to local food chains (birds and other animals eat butterflies), etc… 
    
    “Vanishing Mariposas: U.S. Butterfly Populations Plunge After 20 Years.”

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Beeswarm / dot plot** (a one-dimensional scatter of dots along a horizontal quantitative axis).

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **beeswarm-style jitter/packing** to avoid overlap of dots.
- No faceting, no stacking, and no small multiples.
- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |
| Statistical significance of species trend | Categorical/nominal (binary, as shown) | Outline/stroke around dots (“Outlined species’ trends were statistically significant”) |
| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:
- The y-position does **not** appear to encode a data variable; it is used for collision avoidance / packing only.
- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Beeswarm / dot plot** (a one-dimensional scatter of dots along a horizontal quantitative axis).

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **beeswarm-style jitter/packing** to avoid overlap of dots.
- No faceting, no stacking, and no small multiples.
- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |
| Statistical significance of species trend | Categorical/nominal (binary, as shown) | Outline/stroke around dots (“Outlined species’ trends were statistically significant”) |
| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:
- The y-position does **not** appear to encode a data variable; it is used for collision avoidance / packing only.
- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.
raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    
    I noticed that many butterfly species have declined between 2000 and 2020
    Some species of butterfly have increased
    Orange dots appear more frequently on the negative side of the graph, this might represent more species are declining than they are increasing 
    
    What do you wonder?
    
    What is causing the decrease in butterfly populations?
    Are certain butterfly species more at risk than others?
    What could be helping certain butterfly species increase? Could these factors be hurting other butterfly species?
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    
    This information could help me do some research on which butterfly species are native to Andover, and if their populations are increasing or decreasing.
    
    What's Going On in This Graph?
    
    This graph represents the changes in butterfly species in the United States between 2000 and 2020, it also shows us that many species are currently experiencing a decline in their populations.
    
    Catchy Headline:
    
    The butterfly effect, this time in reverse?

- No faceting, no stacking, and no small multiples.
- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |
| Statistical significance of species trend | Categorical/nominal (binary, as shown) | Outline/stroke around dots (“Outlined species’ trends were statistically significant”) |
| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:
- The y-position does **not** appear to encode a data variable; it is used for collision avoidance / packing only.
- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I am able to see that many species of butterflies have had decreases in their population. While some species were able to grow in population, the majority saw a decrease in abundance. It is interesting how many species have been counted in this chart.
    
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder why there were such drastic changes in abundance. Most of the species saw a decrease in their population with few species showing growth in comparison. I wonder why this occurred and how it relates to the environment as well as what we could do to keep these dying species alive.
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    Butterflies are one of natures greatest beauties and most important species. With their brightly colored wings, they pollinate other plants as they migrate during the changing seasons. As such a vital source of pollination, many plants depend on them to reproduce. Without them, it is possible that not only butterflies, but certain plants may also die, tampering with the ecosystem.  With fewer butterflies being seen in Bergenfield, it shows how we must be more aware of our environment and take better care of nature.
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    ¨Pollinator in Peril¨

- **Beeswarm / dot plot** (a one-dimensional scatter of dots along a horizontal quantitative axis).

- Uses **beeswarm-style jitter/packing** to avoid overlap of dots.
- No faceting, no stacking, and no small multiples.
- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |

| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:
- The y-position does **not** appear to encode a data variable; it is used for collision avoidance / packing only.
- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
    I noticed that there is an unsettling amount of butterflies decreasing and not only this, but also, 3 of the butterfly species that were at the start of the graph are gone towards the middle/end. 
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    I wonder what happened to the butterflies and why did they decline so rapidly, also I wonder what happened to the red and orange species of butterflies that they disappeared so quickly. 
    
    3. How does this relate to you and your community?
    When I was younger, my mother would get us caterpillars to watch them grow and turn into butterflies to eventually release into the wild, to watch and learn about the evolution of  butterflies. This activity would teach me and my brothers many lessons, not only those about the evolution process but also life lessons such as patience and seeing the beauty that change can bring. Seeing the butterflies grow and then releasing them into the wild was always such a fun experience and it is one of the things that made my family and I come together to truly enjoy watching nature and seeing the beauty in things that many people overlook. This issue relates to me because seeing how rapidly the butterflies vanish, it reminds me to hold tighter to the memories that have been created becasue of the butterfly species because one day, it will be rare to see them at all. 
    
    4. Create a headline that captures the graph's main idea
    "Butterflies Gone Missing? What is Happening to the Worlds Population of Butterflies?"

1. What do you notice? 
    I notice how the butterfly population rapidly decreased, and not only a decrease in population but a decrease in specific butterfly species, all the read and orange species in the start of the graph are gone by the time we get to the middle of the graph. 
    
    2. What do you wonder?
    I wonder why the butterfly population is decreasing so rapidly, but I also wonder why specific butterfly species are going extinct. 
    
    
    How does this relate you you and your community?

Looking back at these long-term science experiments, not only did we learn about the process of a butterfly but we also learned more "valuable" lessons. raw_comment:
1. I notice the abundance of orange data points, indicating a negative change in butterfly abundance. More specifically, I see a large number of statistically significant negative changes. This is very concerning, as butterflies are an integral part of our ecosystem, without them, we will be in big trouble.
    2. I have some curiosities regarding the graph choices and the story the data presents. To be completely honest, it took me a little time to figure out what the graph was showing and what everything meant. I don’t have a perfect solution, and I eventually understood its message, but as a statistician, I know data visualization needs to be clear. You can’t assume the viewer will interpret it the same way you do without some guidance. For example, a key for the color gradient could be helpful since it is not explicitly explained, and the color choice is not color-blind friendly. As for the story of the data, I am concerned. Such significant species declines are alarming, no matter the species. My initial assumption is that global warming and harmful agricultural practices are the primary causes.
    3. This data relates to my life because it could be some of my own actions that contribute to this change. While some progress has been made toward a “greener” world, clearly, there is much more work to be done. We need to start while we’re ahead, because the numbers are only going to get worse.
    4. Catchy headline: “Float Like a Butterfly, Stung by Climate Change”

## 1) Chart type
- **Beeswarm / dot plot** (a one-dimensional scatter of dots along a horizontal quantitative axis).

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses **beeswarm-style jitter/packing** to avoid overlap of dots.
- No faceting, no stacking, and no small multiples.
- Dots are arranged along a single horizontal scale, with a separate clustered annotation for **“More than +100%”** at the far right.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Change in butterfly abundance, 2000–20 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Species | Categorical/nominal | One dot per species (individual mark identity) |
| Statistical significance of species trend | Categorical/nominal (binary, as shown) | Outline/stroke around dots (“Outlined species’ trends were statistically significant”) |
| Direction/magnitude grouping of change (negative to positive) | Quantitative | Color/hue of dots (orange for declines, beige near zero, green for increases) |
| More than +100% change | Quantitative threshold/category as displayed | Separate right-side clustered placement with label |

Notes:
- The y-position does **not** appear to encode a data variable; it is used for collision avoidance / packing only.
- The title indicates the time span **2000–20**, but time is presented as context in the title rather than encoded on an axis.
